claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has intrinsically low hardness and moderate strength.
The low hardness and moderate strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed primarily by an absence of pronounced short-range chemical order.
An absence of SRO leaves fewer local obstacles to dislocation motion.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation glide produces high ductility and machinability.
SRO creates nanoscale chemical clusters that act as barriers to dislocations.
Dislocation barriers produced by SRO increase yield strength and hardness while reducing ductility.
The initial material is as-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple solid-solution structure and minimal SRO.
Slow cooling from the solutionizing temperature will promote SRO in CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid quenching from the solutionizing temperature will suppress SRO in CoCrFeNiTi.
Both comparison groups will begin from a homogenized state produced above 1000 °C.
The relevant structural mediator is the degree of nanoscale short-range chemical order.
SRO and random-solid-solution structures can be generated and compared to study the effect of local chemical order on mechanical behavior.
A uniform chemical environment in quenched samples permits easier dislocation glide than an SRO-rich environment.
Non-transforming secondary phases can impede dislocation glide and increase resistance to deformation.
Slow-cooled, SRO-rich CoCrFeNiTi will have greater yield strength and hardness than quenched, SRO-suppressed CoCrFeNiTi.
Slow-cooled, SRO-rich CoCrFeNiTi will have lower ductility than quenched, SRO-suppressed CoCrFeNiTi.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi retained as a simple solid solution without secondary-phase formation or phase separation.
The hypothesis is tested at 25 °C under uniaxial compression up to the elastic/plastic transition.
SRO can be quantified using atom-probe tomography or high-resolution or in-situ transmission electron microscopy.

The mechanism is falsified if confirmed SRO differences produce no statistically significant differences in yield strength, hardness, or ductility, or if the property changes do not correlate with SRO after other factors are excluded.

contradictions.description: Compression is limited to the elastic/plastic transition, but the prediction and falsification rule require comparing ductility or plastic strain. Testing only to the transition cannot establish total ductility or a meaningful reduction in plastic deformation.

The starting as-cast alloy is described as already having minimal SRO, while the controlled comparison is defined from a separate homogenized state. It is therefore unclear whether the as-cast baseline is one of the tested controls or merely a third, structurally distinct condition.
